items.title: 11.1 Scalar And Vector-Valued Functions Of A Single Variable

source_refs.note: Book p. 286: Unit 11 Introduction, r(t) = t i + t^2 j (Figure 11.1) and the satellite helix (Figure 11.2)
Book p. 287-288: heading 11.1 (no own text; sub-topics 11.1.1-11.1.3 on their own pages)

blocks.text: Vector-valued functions return vectors with both magnitude and direction to model multidimensional quantities such as position, velocity, or force in 2D or 3D, unlike scalar functions which give a single value. Their derivative provides the instantaneous rate of change, yielding the velocity vector essential for analyzing motion, with applications in engineering, computer graphics, and physics, from robotic arms to planetary orbits. This chapter covers definitions, component forms, operations, and differentiation techniques for analyzing curves and solving real-world problems involving velocity and acceleration.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
In one sentence: a vector-valued function is a rule that takes one number \(t\) (usually time) and gives back a vector. Think of a GPS tracker: you tell it the time, it tells you where the object is, as a position vector. A scalar function gives back only one number, such as the temperature at that time.
Recall from Grade XI: \(\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\) are the unit vectors along the \(x\)-, \(y\)- and \(z\)-axes. The vector \(a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}\), drawn from the origin, ends at the point \((a, b, c)\). So a position vector and a point carry the same information.

For example, a particle moving along a path in 2D might have its position at time \(t\) given by:
\[\mathbf{r}(t) = t\hat{i} + t^{2}\hat{j}\]
This means at time \(t\), the particle is at the point \((t, t^{2})\) (Figure 11.1).

blocks.alt: Graph of the parabola traced by r(t) = t i + t squared j for t from about minus 3 to 3. Points marked at t = -2 (-2, 4), t = -1 (-1, 1), t = 0 at the origin, t = 1 (1, 1) and t = 2 (2, 4). Arrows on the curve point in the direction of increasing t: down the left branch, through the origin, up the right branch.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to read Figure 11.1: put \(t = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2\) into \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) (table above) and plot the points. The arrows show the direction in which the particle moves as \(t\) increases: it comes down the left branch, passes through the origin at \(t = 0\) and goes up the right branch.
Why a parabola? The components are \(x = t\) and \(y = t^{2}\). Putting \(t = x\) into \(y = t^{2}\) gives \(y = x^{2}\), the parabola you already know. The vector function tells more than the curve: it also tells where the particle is at each moment and which way it is moving.

A real-world example of a vector-valued function in three-dimensional space is the position of a satellite orbiting Earth. Suppose the vector-valued function describes a satellite's position at time \(t\) (in hours):

blocks.text_alt: r of t equals 4000 cos t times i, plus 4000 sin t times j, plus 3000 t times k

blocks.text: Here, the components represent the satellite's coordinates in space: \(x = 4000\cos t\), \(y = 4000\sin t\), and \(z = 3000t\) (in kilometers). The \(x\)- and \(y\)-components model the satellite's circular orbit in the \(xy\)-plane with a radius of 4000 km, while the \(z\)-component indicates a linear ascent along the \(z\)-axis at a rate of 3000 km per hour. This function maps time to a position vector, describing the satellite's trajectory through space, which is essential for tracking and communication in aerospace engineering (Figure 11.2).

blocks.alt: Three-dimensional sketch of a helix around the z-axis. The dashed circle of radius 4000 km lies in the xy-plane; the curve starts at (4000, 0, 0) at t = 0 and winds upward twice, with points marked at t = 0, pi/2, pi, 3pi/2, 2pi, 5pi/2, 3pi, 7pi/2 and 4pi. A z scale on the right runs from 0 to 40000 km in steps of 5000.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.2: helix of the satellite r(t) = (4000 cos t) i + (4000 sin t) j + 3000t k for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4π, z scale 0 to 40000 km (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Figure 11.2 the scale on the \(z\)-axis is printed (from the top) 3500, 3000, 25000, 20000, 15000, 10000, 5000, 0. The marks go up in equal steps of 5000 km, so the top two should read 35000 and 30000 (one zero is missing in each). Our figure uses the correct scale; it runs up to 40000 km because at \(t = 4\pi\) the height is \(3000 \times 4\pi \approx 37699\) km.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is the orbit a circle of radius 4000 km? For every \(t\),
\[x^{2} + y^{2} = 4000^{2}(\cos^{2} t + \sin^{2} t)\]
\[= 4000^{2}\]
so the point \((x, y)\) always stays 4000 km from the \(z\)-axis.
Why 3000 km per hour? \(z = 3000t\) grows by 3000 every time \(t\) grows by 1 hour.
One full circle takes \(t = 2\pi \approx 6.28\) hours, and in that time the satellite rises \(3000 \times 2\pi \approx 18850\) km. Circle plus a steady climb gives a helix (the shape of a spring or a spiral staircase). The numbers are a simplified textbook model; the aim is to see how three scalar components work together as one vector.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A vector-valued function takes one number \(t\) and returns a vector; a scalar function returns one number.
2. \(\mathbf{r}(t) = t\hat{i} + t^{2}\hat{j}\) puts the particle at the point \((t, t^{2})\); its path is the parabola \(y = x^{2}\).
3. Satellite: \(x = 4000\cos t\), \(y = 4000\sin t\) give a circle of radius 4000 km; \(z = 3000t\) gives a steady climb; together they give a helix.
4. To see the path, put several values of \(t\) into \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) and plot the points in order of \(t\); the order gives the direction of motion.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Thinking the vector \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) and the point are unrelated: the position vector drawn from the origin ends exactly at the point.
2. Assuming the \(x\)-component is always \(t\): in \(t\hat{i} + t^{2}\hat{j}\) it is, but for the satellite \(x = 4000\cos t\).
3. Using degrees inside \(\cos t\) and \(\sin t\): in calculus \(t\) is in radians (here \(t\) also counts hours).
